Boardgame dating app?
I've been talking to a lot of people in the boardgame community, and I've noticed that a lot of people have a hard time finding people to play boardgames with that not only enjoy the same types of games as them, but also play at the same level of intensity as they do (more social playing vs. hyperfocused on winning). People even mention that they go to different game shops or conventions but struggle to find boardgame buddies that they connect with.

I was curious what yall would think of an app that functioned like a dating app, but was designed to help people find those around them who enjoyed the same games as them.

I have 2 different ideas and I was curious what you thought of these on a scale of 1-10 (1=dumb 10=really good idea)

Swiping through profiles that mention their favorite games and genres. (eg tinder, bumble, hinge, etc but for finding a boardgame buddy)

Swiping through nearby hosted game nights. Someone could create an event that names the game, the date and time, and what city its in (unless you want to host it in a public location), and how many people you are looking to have join. Then a person swiping though would be able to swipe yes on a game night to connect with the organizer and get more details.

Is one idea better than the other, or do they just both suck?

I finally updated my "7 Wonders Score Sheet" Android app after a decade

I made the first version of 7 Wonders Score Sheet back _13 years ago_ and posted about it here on r/boardgames; I then updated it a bit into 2016 for Leaders and Cities expansions which were then-new, but embarrassingly, its been a decade since the last update. About a year or two ago, Google Play took it down for being so stale; tho by then it'd blown past 100k downloads!

Apologies for the self-promotion and all, but its a free app with no ads, no analytics, no accounts, and no internet interaction whatsoever that I made because I just really like 7 Wonders and am a full time android dev as my day-job. The latest update has import/export data backup, a quick-flow first-launch experience to dial in all your settings to get right to scoring, supports all the official expansions, all the official Wonders, an interactive explainer of how science scoring works (a lot of people seem to get that wrong?) and of course rich persistent stats for players, matches, wonders (both sides now!), streaks, etc; and since the last update there's a second edition of the game, so there's both 1st and 2nd edition game support with various subtle UI tweaks.

Figured I just drop a post to follow up on my 13 year old post for the app!

Lemme know if you have any issues or feature ideas; I tried to incorporate most the feedback I'd recieved over the years in this update.

someone please help me find this card game
What I personally call it is 3 and an ace but I cant find any trace of it anywhere online.

The aim of the game is to get 3 cards of the same number (2 of hearts, 2 of spades, 2 clubs), and an ace of any suit. You can also do a run.

The game can have a minimum of 2 players and then upwards of as many as wanted. Everyone is dealt 4 cards each except one person who gets 5. The rest of the deck is then set face down in the middle of the space (or wherever everyone can reach).

The person who has 5 cards then throws one away that they don't need / doesn't add anything to their hand. This card is placed face up beside the other, face down, deck of cards. The next person to go can either take that card if they need it, or can pick one up from the face down deck. They can then throw this card away or keep it, then the cycle repeats for the next players.

The game ends when someone either gets 3 cards of the same number and an ace, or a run and an ace.

I've looked this game up a million times and I can't find anything about it anywhere. If it helps any, I learned it from my mother whos from Glasgow, so it could maybe originate from surrounding areas? (Greenock, Port Glasgow, Gourock).

Orcquest Warpath: orcs vs humans, kraft and stealth crawling

Dungeon crawler in unusual reversed setting: protagonists are orcs, who went on quest to save orc race from human invasion. And their enemies are traditionally good races: humans, elves and dwarves (in later campaigns). Although there are some campaigns about classic enemies as well - monsters, undead, etc.

Gameplay will feel familiar to people familiar with genre: your characters have 2 action points and several possible actions to choose from - move, attack, use special abilities, etc. You move across the board, enter rooms (funnily enough, enemy`s facing is determined by roll of die, so you often get opportunity to stab unexpecting guard right in the ass), clean them from enemies by rolling custom dice whose colors depend on your weapon, and try to complete mission`s goal (and preferably secondary goal - usually kill some important person - to gain bonus).

The interesting feature is that actions are on cards, and you can make them stronger either by spending more action points (but it is really expensive) or preferably badass points. This resource you gain for killing stronger enemies, oneshotting enemies and doing other cool stuff. They also can be spent on buying stronger skill cards, so you need to weight what is more important: temporary benefits right now or skill later.

Also, if your orc managed to deal damage with two attacks during turn, he/she can use skill with keyword "combo 1" for free then. And if it damages as well, then he can use "combo 2" for free. You do not manage to create such powerful chain often, but when you do, you feel very badass. Really fun way to power up.

Another feature is kraft system. You can find resources on enemies bodies and searching dungeons, and then use them to create new weapon, or upgrade existing one. Some upgrades feel very cool, like lifesteal enchantment, for example.

There also stealth enement present: enemies can be in passive or alert state. There is alert tracker. And some enemies patrol the board in groups (which get tougher with each mission, of course), moving each turn depending on drawn cards. If they see you, fight begins, and one of enemies will try to ran to bell and ring it. If he succeeds, alarm sounds, and patrols become very tough to deal with, so does your life overall.

Another thematic touch is that every turn orcs draw cards from event deck, which can make them start brawl with each other or do other fun/useful/harmful stuff.

Artwork is pretty nice, and there are humor elements in the story, which does not take itself too seriously.

Characters themselves are not radically different, but still have distinct playstyle (base 4 orcs are classic archer, warrior, rogue, mage) and grow in power significantly over the course of campaigning, learning new roles: leader who buffs others, mobile shooter and so on.

So Orcquest is quite fun dungeon crawler in (mostly) classic style, but with original setting and a lot of thematic stuff. Overall I enjoyed it.

As for cons, they are significant, too:

Orcs grow in power too quickly because of kraft, and missions become too easy. Especially since the way combat system works in this game, weak enemies have little chance of damaging someone with defense of stronger color.

While gameplay is not fiddly, setup takes a while because of tons of tokens to place on board, and a lot of character cards: skills, weapons, resources... Requires very big table.

Stealth system does not work well; patrols activate too randomly and inconsistently, often you may not encounter them during mission at all. Does not feel like much of stealth game.

Rules are often ambigious or hard to grasp, and leave room to intrepretation.

Also in case if you try to solo game, you will have to manage 4 characters. Even though they are simple on their own, it still means a lot of cards to track, especially in later missions.

Turns out the people that are into Board Games tend to look for either the more "immersive" games like The LoTR and Dune games, or are looking for more "friendly" themes to play with family and friends like Fliptoons, Flip 7, and just the usual Catan/Monopoly. Do you plan an “opener” and a “closer” for game night?
My board game group plays multiple games in a night and usually doesn't repeat/overlap games from week to week. I've noticed a trend emerging on the types of games we play as we start vs end the night.

Opener: Something quick and light while people settle in. Easy to join mid-game, ideally under 15 minutes.

Main event: The bigger game everyone came for.

Closer: Something short and fun/less competitive to end on a high note.

Running a few game tables recently made me realize the opener matters more than I thought. A good one gets people talking and settles the “I’m not a game person” crowd before the main game starts.

Tidal Blades 2: Wardian Sky - a playtesters review

Hi,

I'm a volunteer playtester for Tidal Blades 2: Wardian Sky.

I've not received payment in any form from the creators or publisher.

As a fan of Tidal Blades 2 I merely applied for play testing, the same as everyone else could do, through one of their Kickstarter updates.

Tidal Blades 2

is a dungeon crawler, that stands out through its unique ocean centric fantasy world.
The innovative grid based card play offers an incredibly deep puzzle without having a high complexity.
Each turn a player places a single card on a grid.
Then the player can activate the placed card together with some cards, that were placed in previous rounds.

Its greatest strength is the variety in enemies and scenarios.
Even the smallest enemies have unique behaviors that are thematically tied to them leaving an impression.

Tidal Blades 2: Wardian Sky is the first expansion and adds quite a few things.

New Unique Hero Abilities.

Each hero is getting a new unique ability consisting of a small board with the rules and some tokens. The abilities fit the characters very well both thematically and mechanically. For example, Dust, a hero that is dancing through the enemies with her 2 swords, got 2 tokens representing her weapons.
She can exhaust the tokens to enhance her attacks, or use them defensively to parry attacks.

New starting decks.

The expansion is adding a new starting deck for each character.
Together with the unique abilities, the new decks are the biggest improvement for me.
Before each character already had some cards that mechanically reflected their personalities.
But in the base game the characters felt more similar to each other with slight variations.
The expansion on the other hand manages to make every hero feel uniquely distinct.

New ability cards.

The expansion is adding a new type of cards that can be obtained by simple crafting.
They are more powerful and offer access to a new type of die.
This die can be used for devasting attacks and trigger abilities that are tied to the new cards.

New enemies.

As every other aspect in this game, the new enemies all offer a very unique feeling.
It's amazing how mechanically each enemy type has ther own specialities that fit them thematically.

10 (+2 bonus) scenarios.

10 scenarios sounds like a small amount,
but Tidal Blade 2 has its focus on extreme variety in scenarios.
Other games with 50+ scenarios can often feel repetitive after a while. The Scenarios I've played so far, all feel fresh and very memorable.
Every single one offered multiple exciting surprises.

Summary.

The expansion is keeping the core concept and improving the most important aspects of the base game.

Even after playing the same scenarios over and over again for testing, the puzzle stayed fun and I was looking forward to the next run.

10/10

If you have any questions, I'll try to answer them as long as the NDA allows for that.

You Should Avoid Everything Epic Board Games

This warning post is directly in response to the Secrets of the Lost Tomb - Epic Remastered Edition - 10 Year Anniversary crowdfunding campaign on Gamefound. I have posted on BGG, but I am also posting here to give visibility to anyone who may make the same mistake I did.

For context, I am a backer who late pledged in July of 2025, while the campaign ended in Oct. 2023 with a 18 month fulfillment timeline. The late pledge is still ongoing with fullfillment maybe in Q1 2027.

I like many other backers have requested a pledge cancellation and refund (minus gamefound fees). Everything Epic (specifically the CEO Chris) has been making excuses and lying to backers about giving refunds for pledge cancellations for at least the past 6-8 months.

You might be asking yourself: Well it's crowdfunding, there is no expectation of refunds being given so why are you writing this?

While that is correct, I would offer a few counterpoints:

Any experienced crowdfunding creator gives refunds (minus fees) these days. Crowdfunding from a "over 25 successful campaigns" company is just a glorified preorder rather than supporting a small creator's first project.

The campaign is on track to be 2 years late for fulfillment. It's happened before with plenty of campaigns, but having a small amount of backers through financial hardship, leaving the hobby, or simply no longer being interested in the game wanting to cancel and be refunded is a pretty reasonable expectation over the course of 3.5 years.

Chris has repeatedly lied to backers about giving refunds. Various excuses such as "I'm busy", "I'm the only person at the company", "Email me and I'll look into it", "I can't locate your info", "I haven't received an email/message", "Go to our discord", "You can reach me 24/7", "I'll look into this right away", etc. are all over Gamefound, BGG, and the official discord. As an added bonus I have personally seen him delete refund request messages and complaints in the discord.

Chris will not respond to emails or Gamefound messages. Including Gamefound support reaching out to have him contact backers. The only things he responds to are public messages, with one of his excuses. I have personally sent a Gamefound message, contacted Gamefound support, and sent 2 emails directly to Chris.

If he had simply been honest about not giving refunds I wouldn't even be making this post. I could respect that or at the very least understand it. It is after all in line with crowdfunding at its core, regardless of modern practices.

I however, take issue with the lying to backers for the past 6+ months and not responding to emails. I also find it distasteful to have a Refunds and Cancellation section in your campaign while outright ignoring any backers attempt at one.

His actions also directly go against this excerpt from the campaigns Risks and Challenges section which is laughable to even see considering where we stand today:

"We endeavor to please our backers in any way we can! We want you to enjoy our games, stories, and creations to their fullest. If there is anything that we can ever do to make your experience better, we're always here to help! Our Motto is "Of the Gamer, by the Gamer, and For the Gamer!" we know what it's like to be Ignored by Project Creators, never to get an email back from a Game Company, to have to post on a blog to get a response... We're not Like that... Here's the President of our Company's email... Chris@EverythingEpic.us. You can email me directly for anything you ever need, and I will always respond to you directly and help in any way I can."

I do not believe it is foolish or wrong to expect someone to be true to their word and to have integrity, especially when you are giving them a decent sum of money for a product.

I would recommend anyone avoid supporting this company and any crowdfunding campaigns they have. Maybe plenty of the 25 have been fine, but if this is how they act on arguably the biggest one they've had, I believe that says all it needs to.

If you made it this far, I appreciate you taking the time to read it all, thank you

Edit;

I emailed Chris for the final time. I do truly hope he meant what he said in his apology. Mistakes happen and life can get away from you before you know it, but I can't only take him at his word. Unless action follows, that will just be a meaningless reply. I also do want other backers to get a response and have a good campaign late or otherwise. In the end as long as it is a good game, the timeline isn't an issue really. At the same time, all the best campaigns I have been a part of have never had a communication issue like this. It is his every right to not give refunds if he chooses because that's what the backers sign up for. At the same time, having difficulties whether professional or personally shouldn't fall on the backers to not have a good experience with the project they are hoping is good. Just because they can fail and there is no guarantee of anything, doesn't diminish any valid points I made. Whether you agree with me or not, there is some change that should happen.

Edit 2:

True to his word he did refund me, even though he didn't have to. Thank you for that and I do hope you are able to get this to backers soon. While my circumstances may have changed, I did not originally back this for no reason. I think it will still be a great game and I wish you success with it!

Where’s the sweet spot between accessibility, strategy and player interaction?
One thing I’ve been thinking about lately is what makes a board game work well with people who enjoy playing games socially but don’t necessarily play modern board games on a regular basis.
Some of my personal favourites are games like Inis, Dune: Imperium – Uprising and recently The Old King’s Crown.

What I enjoy about these games is the meaningful decisions, strategic depth and, perhaps most importantly, the interaction between players. I like games where you’re constantly reacting to what others are doing, negotiating the board state, and trying to outmanoeuvre your opponents rather than simply optimising your own engine.

The challenge is that these qualities don’t always translate particularly well to a casual game night with people who aren’t used to modern board games. A game can be relatively straightforward to learn but still demand a fair amount of experience to understand what makes it interesting. On the other hand, making everything too light can leave you with a game that feels a little too random or multiplayer-solitaire for my taste.

It makes me wonder what actually defines that sweet spot: games that are approachable enough to get to the table with a mixed group, but still offer meaningful strategic decisions and genuine interaction from the very first play.

I’m curious how others approach this. Do you think it’s primarily about simplifying the rules, shortening the playtime, reducing the number of mechanisms, or something else entirely? And do you find that certain types of player interaction are easier for newcomers to engage with than others?

I’d be particularly interested in hearing how others balance their own preference for deeper, more interactive games with the reality of playing with less experienced groups.

Board game tools and sites (2026)
I try board gaming tools so you don't have to. I have updated the list from last year with new entries and changes.

Statistics

BoredGamerTools is very easy to use and has a ton of cool visualization. You just plug in your BGG username. Free with a $3 premium option.

CrdBrd has some interesting concepts with average enjoyment and breaks down board games into Luck Factor, Player Interaction, Immersion, Complexity, Stategic Depth and Rules overhead. It is one of the more complicated sites and I have often encountered bugs but there is so much to look at.

GeekGroup.app just requires your BGG username and then you are ready to watch the graphs. Free with a $2+ premium option.

Collections

Kallax.io has the best collection viewer. They group expansions together with the base game and filters can apply across multiple collections.

HeresMyShelf is good for sharing collections in an instagram-like grid. The search and filtering is not as powerful but the collection view is nice and simple and with easy access to custom lists.

GeekGroup.app is great for sharing your collection and they also group expansions and show your rating relative to BGG. Only downside is you need to update in BGG and then wait for the weekly sync (or pay).

Play Online

Board Game Arena has a 1000+ games to play for free. The UI is a bit dated, but the site works and is very active.

Table Top Simulator is a steam game where you download the games as DLCs. It's paid and the quality of games very but generally good fun.

Table Topia is offers a mix of free and premium games. Their web player is 3D and generally high quality.

Play Tracking

BG Stats is still the best here. It is paid but one of the few sites that can actually push to BoardGameGeek and not only import.

NemeStats integrates with both BG Stats and BGG. It is open source, free and does not serve ads. The interface is a bit old school but it works well.

BG Catalog is the best free alternative for mobile. It is free but with advertisement. They got their BGG API key back, so all good.

Events

AfterGame has a lot of features for larger events and they started supporting event ticket sales directly in the app this yaer. Their UI will feel very intuitive if you are used to Meetup or Facebook events.

Kallax.io is better for smaller event. Voting for what to play and when to met but they don't support multi-table events very well. They do not require an account to participate and vote.

Meetup does not have any board game specific features but it is used by so many that the visibility it brings to your events alone makes it worthy for a spot on the list.

Questions about Vantage
Hello! A few questions came up during our three-player game of Vantage yesterday.

Another player and I were at the same location, which had a Move action that allowed him to enter a portal. He entered the portal and moved to a new location, while I stayed behind with the original location card.

1. I could have moved with him if I’d wanted to, since he took a Move action, correct?

2. At the new location, he took a Scan action. If I later entered the portal and reached that same location, would I be allowed to take Scan too? Or would his action make only Scan unavailable to me, or prevent me from taking any location action there?

3. What if we were at the same location and he took a Help action whose result instructed him to move to another location? Could I still move with him, even though it wasn’t a Move action?

Crowdfunding Horror Stories
I was just updating my personal tracker for outstanding crowdfunded games and started looking at some of the fulfillment trends for projects I've backed. I usually do not back massive projects (games with lots of minis, etc) which I know usually run into more production delays than smaller campaigns. And I back far fewer projects than some: 30-40 over the past five years or so. So my sample size is fairly small. I consider myself very lucky that I've never backed a project (yet) that has failed to deliver.

Although I've been waiting on a few games for 2-3 years, the usual funded-to-arrival time is around 12-18 months for projects I've backed. However, only one game I've backed in the past five years has met it's originally-stated fulfillment goal. Almost every single one has pushed back fulfillment for one reason or another.

What are your worst crowdfunding experiences for games? I want to hear about ridiculous delays, poor communication, awful quality, and everything else.
